[ASSISTANT_SAID] In philosophy, "givenness" refers to the quality of something being "given" to us in our experience, associated with the phenomenological tradition.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Givenness emphasizes the subjective nature of our experience and the importance of taking immediate experience seriously.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Facticity refers to the concrete, factual aspects of our existence, including our physical body, social context, and historical situation.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Givenness and facticity contribute to our overall experience of the world, with facticity shaping how things are given to us.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Eidetic reduction is a method in phenomenology used to uncover the essential features of a given experience or object.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Eidetic reduction involves imaginative variation to isolate necessary features of an experience.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] The term "immanent" refers to something inherent within a particular domain or context, as opposed to transcending it.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] In phenomenology, objects are immanent within our experience, constituted by the acts of consciousness.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Important quotes from Husserl's works on intentionality include: "Every mental act is directed toward an object, every mental act intends something." (Logical Investigations, 1900-1901)

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Important quotes from Husserl's works on the method of reduction include: "To the things themselves! Back to the things themselves!" (Ideas I, 1913)

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Important quotes from Husserl's works on consciousness include: "Consciousness is always consciousness of something, it is essentially intentional." (Ideas I, 1913)

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Important quotes from Husserl's works on experience include: "Experience is the foundation of all knowledge, it is the primary source of all our beliefs and judgments." (Logical Investigations, 1900-1901)

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Important quotes from Husserl's works on the natural attitude include: "The natural attitude is the seat of all prejudices and errors." (The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, p. 67)

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Sartre's philosophy emphasizes that human beings are fundamentally free and conscious subjects, and that this subjectivity gives meaning to the world.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Sartre argues that subjective experience is what defines us as human beings and is the source of all value and meaning in our lives.
